'''Heart of Midlothian Football Club''', commonly known as '''Hearts''', is a professional [[Association football|football]] club in [[Edinburgh]], Scotland. The team competes in the {{Scottish football updater|HeartofM}}, the top division of [[Scottish football league system|Scottish football]]. Hearts, the oldest football club in the Scottish capital,<ref>{{cite book |last= Bowie|first=Andrew-Henry |date=2011 |title=Two miles to Tynecastle |location=Clacton on Sea |publisher=Apex}}</ref> was formed in 1874, its name influenced by [[Walter Scott]]'s novel ''[[The Heart of Midlothian]]'' (1818).<ref name="1874-1884"/> The club crest is based on the [[Heart of Midlothian (Royal Mile)|''Heart of Midlothian'' mosaic]] on the city's [[Royal Mile]]; the team's colours are maroon and white.<ref name="1874-1884"/> Their local rivals are [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]], with whom they contest the [[Edinburgh derby]].

Hearts have played home matches at [[Tynecastle Park]] since 1886.<ref name = "Inglis447">{{harvnb|Inglis|1996|p=447}}</ref> After the ground was converted into an all-seater stadium in 1994, it now has a capacity of {{SPFL-stadiums|hearts}}<ref name=capacity/> following the completion of a rebuilt main stand in 2017. They have training facilities at the [[Oriam]], Scotland's national performance centre for sport, where they also run their [[Heart of Midlothian F.C. Reserves and Academy|youth academy]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.scottishfa.co.uk/performance/oriam/ |title=Oriam - The jewel in the crown of Scottish sport |work=Scottish FA |access-date=24 September 2018}}</ref>

Hearts have won the [[List of Scottish football champions|Scottish league championship]] four times, most recently in [[1959–60 Scottish Division One|1959–60]], when they also retained the [[1959 Scottish League Cup final|Scottish League Cup]] to complete a [[Double (association football)#League & League Cup Double|League and League Cup double]] – the only club outside of the [[Old Firm]] to achieve such a feat.

The club's most successful period was under former player turned manager [[Tommy Walker (footballer, born 1915)|Tommy Walker]] from the early 1950s to mid 1960s, during which they won two league titles and five major cups and finished inside the league's top four positions for 11 consecutive seasons. [[Jimmy Wardhaugh]], [[Willie Bauld]] and [[Alfie Conn Sr.]], known as the Terrible Trio, were forwards at the start of this period with wing half linchpins [[Dave Mackay]] and [[John Cumming (Scottish footballer)|John Cumming]]. Wardhaugh was part of another notable Hearts attacking trinity in the [[1957–58 Scottish Division One|1957–58]] league winning side: along with [[Jimmy Murray (footballer, born 1933)|Jimmy Murray]] and [[Alex Young (footballer, born 1937)|Alex Young]],<ref name=lh1956>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/sea/1957-58.html|title=1957-58|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> they set the record for the number of goals scored in a Scottish top-flight winning campaign (132) and also became the only side to finish a season in the Scottish top tier with a goal difference exceeding 100 (+103).

Hearts have won the [[Scottish Cup]] eight times, most recently in [[2012 Scottish Cup final|2012]] after a 5–1 victory over Hibernian.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/18044372|title=Hibernian 1 Hearts 5|date=19 May 2012|work=BBC Sport|access-date=22 May 2012}}</ref> They have since been runners up in [[2019 Scottish Cup final|2019]], [[2020 Scottish Cup final|2020]] and [[2022 Scottish Cup final|2022]]. All four of Hearts' [[Scottish League Cup]] triumphs came under Walker, most recently a 1–0 victory against [[Kilmarnock F.C.|Kilmarnock]] in [[1962 Scottish League Cup final|1962]]. Their most recent League Cup Final appearance was in [[2013 Scottish League Cup final|2013]], where they lost 3–2 to [[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]].

In 1958, Heart of Midlothian became the third [[Football in Scotland|Scottish]] and fifth [[Football in the United Kingdom|British]] team to compete in [[UEFA#Competitions|European competition]]. The club reached the quarter-finals of the [[1988–89 UEFA Cup]], losing to [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] 2–1 on aggregate.

== History ==
{{See also|List of Heart of Midlothian F.C. seasons}}

=== Early years ===
The club was formed by a group of friends from the Heart of Midlothian Quadrille Assembly Club.<ref name="1874-1884" /> The group of friends bought a ball before playing local rules football at the Tron from where they were directed by a local policeman to The Meadows to play. Local rules football was a mix of rugby and association football.<ref name="1874-1884" /> In December 1873 a match was held between XIs selected by Mr Thomson from [[Queen's Park F.C.|Queen's Park]] and Mr Gardner from [[Clydesdale F.C.|Clydesdale]] at Raimes Park in [[Bonnington, Edinburgh|Bonnington]].<ref name="P56">{{cite book | title=McCrae's Battalion | last=Alexander | first=Jack | page=56 | isbn=1-84018-707-7| year=2003 | publisher=Mainstream |place=Edinburgh and London }}</ref> This was the first time that association rules had been seen in Edinburgh. Members from the dance club viewed the match and in 1874 decided to adopt the Association rules.<ref name="p24">{{cite book | url=http://www.londonhearts.com/images/mack02/pages/p024.htm |page=24 |place=London |publisher=Stanley Paul | title=The Hearts | via=London Hearts | first=Albert |last=Mackie | access-date=10 October 2011}}</ref> The new side was Heart of Mid-Lothian Football Club.<ref name="1874-1884" /> The exact date of the club's formation was never recorded; however, 1874 is regarded as the year of formation as it was when association rules were taken on,<ref name="1874-1884" /> although [[Tom Purdie]] claimed the club was formed in 1873.<ref name="P27">{{cite web | url=http://www.londonhearts.com/images/mack02/pages/p027.htm |page=27 | title=The Hearts | via=London Hearts | first=Albert |last=Mackie |place=London |publisher=Stanley Paul | access-date=10 October 2011}}</ref> The earliest mention of "Heart of Midlothian" in a sporting context is a report in ''[[The Scotsman]]'' newspaper from 20 July 1864 of ''The Scotsman'' vs Heart of Mid-Lothian at cricket. It is not known if this was the same club who went on to form the football club, but it was common for football clubs in those days to play other sports as well.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/images/1864/1864072001.jpg |title=From 20 July 1864 of the Scotsman| publisher= London Hearts Supporter Club|access-date=13 June 2012}}</ref>

The club took its name from historic county [[Midlothian]], dating from the [[Middle Ages]], as well as the 1860 ''[[Heart of Midlothian (Royal Mile)|Heart of Midlothian]]'' mosaic on the [[Royal Mile]], which marks the historic entrance to the [[Old Tolbooth, Edinburgh|Old Tolbooth]] jail;<ref name="1874-1884">{{cite web|first1=David |last1=Speed |url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20061108/1874-1884_2241543_924903 |title=History: 1874–1884 |publisher=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |access-date=21 August 2010 |last2=Knight |first2=Alex |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110211181112/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20061108/1874-1884_2241543_924903 |archive-date=11 February 2011 }}</ref> the jail was demolished in 1817 but was kept fresh in the mind by [[Walter Scott]]'s 1818 novel ''[[The Heart of Midlothian]]''.<ref>{{cite book|url=http://londonhearts.com/images/mack02/pages/p029.htm|title=The Hearts: The story of the Heart of Midlothian F.C.|first=Albert|last=Mackie|year=1959|location=London|publisher=Stanley Paul|page=29}} {{ASIN|B0000CKD66|country=uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=McCrae's Battalion |last=Alexander |first=Jack |isbn=1-84018-707-7 |page=55 |year=2003 |publisher=Mainstream }}</ref>

[[File:Hearts team 1875.jpg|thumb|The 1875 Hearts team with the original white shirt]]
Led by captain Tom Purdie the club played its matches in the East Meadows<ref name="P56" /> and in 1875 Hearts became members of the [[Scottish Football Association]] (SFA) and were founder members of the Edinburgh Football Association.<ref name="1874-1884" /> By becoming members of the SFA Hearts were able to play in the [[Scottish Cup]] for the first time. Hearts played against [[3rd Edinburgh Rifle Volunteers F.C.]] in October 1875 at Craigmount Park<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/187510161.html|title=Games: Sat 16 Oct 1875   |publisher= Hearts of London Supporter Club|access-date=13 June 2012}}</ref> in Edinburgh. The game ended in a scoreless draw. A replay was held at the Meadows which again finished 0–0. Under rules at the time both clubs progressed to the next round with Hearts losing out to Drumpellier in the next round.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/scotcuphistfull.html|title=Scotland – Cup Results 1873/74-1877/78 and 1889/90-1995/96|access-date= 13 June 2012|first= Dinant|last= Abbink|date=  2 May 2007}}</ref>

In the [[1884–85 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|1884–85]] season, clubs in Scotland struggled to attract quality players who preferred to play professionally in England.<ref name="1874-1884" /> After an 11–1 win in the [[Scottish Cup]] over Dunfermline<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/188410041.html | title=Sat 04 Oct 1884 Scottish Cup Dunfermline 1 Hearts 11 | publisher=London Hearts | access-date=10 October 2011}}</ref> a protest was raised against the club for fielding two professional players, which was against the rules at the time.<ref name="1874-1884" /> Hearts were suspended by the SFA for two years - the first ever suspension of an SFA club.<ref name="P20">{{cite book | url=http://www.londonhearts.com/images/reid1924/pages/docu0011.htm | title=The Story of 'The Hearts': A Fifty Years' Retrospect 1874–1924 |date=1924 | via=London Hearts |place=Edinburgh |publisher=Heart of Midlothian FC | first=William |last=Reid | access-date=10 October 2011}}</ref> They were readmitted after a change of the club's committee.<ref name="1874-1884" />

=== Early success ===
Hearts had considerable success in the early years of the [[Scottish Football League]], winning the league championship in [[1894–95 in Scottish football|1895]] and [[1895–96 in Scottish football|1896]]. They also won four [[Scottish Cup]]s in a 15-year period from 1891 to 1906. The team played against [[Sunderland A.F.C.|Sunderland]] in the [[1895 World Championship (football)|1894–95 World Championship]], but lost with a 5–3 score.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2020/apr/25/even-when-sunderland-ruled-the-globe-club-world-cups-were-controversial|title=Sunderland's Victorian all-stars blazed trail for money's rule of football |work=The Guardian |author=Jonathan Wilson|date=25 April 2020|access-date=16 May 2020}}</ref> Hearts did win the World Championship title in 1902, beating [[Tottenham Hotspur]] 3–1 in [[Tynecastle Park]], after a 0–0 in London a few months earlier.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/190201021.html|title=1902-01-02 Thu Hearts 3 Tottenham Hotspur 1|website=Londonhearts.com}}</ref>

=== Hearts in World War I ===
[[File:The Heart of Midlothian War Memorial.jpg|right|thumb|125px|Hearts War Memorial]]
{{Main|Heart of Midlothian F.C. and World War I|McCrae's Battalion}}
{{cquote|''Do not ask where Hearts are playing and then look at me askance. If it's football that you're wanting, you must come with us to France!''|author=[[George McCrae (politician)|Sir George McCrae]]}}
In November 1914, Heart of Midlothian comfortably led the First Division,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20101026/contalmaison-and-a-tribute-to-mccraes_2241384_2190827 |title=Contalmaison and a tribute to McCrae's |publisher=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |work=Hearts News |date=26 October 2010 |access-date=9 October 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101029204725/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20101026/contalmaison-and-a-tribute-to-mccraes_2241384_2190827 |archive-date=29 October 2010 }}</ref> having started the [[1914–15 in Scottish football|1914–15 season]] with eight straight victories, including a 2–0 defeat of reigning champions [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/191408151.html | title=Sat 15 Aug 1914 Division 1 Hearts 2 Celtic 0 | publisher=London Hearts | access-date=21 October 2011}}</ref>

This streak coincided with the beginning of [[World War I]] and the start of a public debate upon the morality of continuing professional football while young soldiers were dying on the front-line. A motion was placed before the [[Scottish Football Association]] to postpone the season, with one of its backers, [[Airdrieonians F.C. (1878)|Airdrieonians]] chairman Thomas Forsyth declaring that ''"playing football while our men are fighting is repugnant"''.<ref name="ballot">''McCrae's Battalion'', 15</ref> While this motion was defeated at the [[ballot box]], with the SFA opting to wait for War Office advice, the East London philanthropist [[Frederick Nicholas Charrington]] was orchestrating a public campaign to have professional football in Britain suspended, and achieving great popular support for his cause.<ref name="Charrington">''McCrae's Battalion'', 21–24</ref> The prime tactic of Charrington's campaign was to shame football players and officials into action through public and private denouncement. In response, sixteen players from Hearts enlisted in [[George McCrae (politician)|Sir George McCrae]]'s new volunteer battalion, joining en masse on 25 November 1914. The battalion was to become the 16th Royal Scots and was the first to earn the "footballer's battalion" sobriquet. The group of volunteers also contained some 500 Hearts supporters and ticket-holders, 150 followers of Hibernian and a number of professional footballers from Raith Rovers, Falkirk and Dunfermline.<ref name="Museum">{{cite web| title=Soccer Soldiers: Footballers go to war| work=The National Army Museum| url=http://www.national-army-museum.ac.uk/exhibitions/football/page2.shtml| access-date=19 March 2007| url-status=dead| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071006001158/http://www.national-army-museum.ac.uk/exhibitions/football/page2.shtml| archive-date=6 October 2007| df=dmy-all}}</ref>

Military training was thus added to the Hearts players football training regime, and the side had a 20-game unbeaten run between October and February.<ref name="Season">{{cite web|title=Scotland 1914–15| work=The RSSSF| url=https://www.rsssf.org/tabless/scot15.html | access-date=19 March 2007}}</ref> However, exhaustion from their army exertions, twice including 10-hour nocturnal-marches the night before a league game,<ref name="training">''McCrae's Battalion'', 95–99</ref> eventually led to a drop in form, as several enlisted players missed key games. Defeats to [[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] and Morton allowed Celtic to usurp the ''Maroons'' and eventually claim the league title by 4 points.<ref name="Season"/>

The war claimed the lives of seven first team players: [[Duncan Currie]], John Allan, James Boyd, [[Tom Gracie]], [[Ernest Ellis]], [[James Speedie]] and [[Harry Wattie]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/page/WarMemorial/0,,10289,00.html |title=The Proudest Moment of a Proud Club |publisher=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |work=Hearts News |access-date=12 October 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110921151637/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/page/WarMemorial/0%2C%2C10289%2C00.html |archive-date=21 September 2011 }}</ref> as well as former player [[David Philip]].

There are two war memorials to mark this period; The [[McCrae's Battalion Great War Memorial]] in [[Contalmaison]] and the Heart of Midlothian War Memorial in [[Haymarket, Edinburgh|Haymarket]], Edinburgh donated to the city by the club in 1922.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/heart-of-midlothian-war-memorial-moved-for-edinburgh-trams-1.909193 | title=Heart of Midlothian war memorial moved for Edinburgh trams | publisher=The Herald | work=Herald Scotland | date=4 May 2009 | access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref> The latter was placed in storage due to the [[Edinburgh Trams]] work<ref>{{cite news | url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/edinburgh_and_east/8008214.stm | title=War memorial moved for tram works | publisher=British Broadcasting Corporation |work=BBC News | date=20 April 2009 | access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref> but has now been replaced a little to the east of its previous position. A further memorial commemorating the 1914 Hearts team has been proposed by the club.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110831/hearts-1914-memorial-trust_2241384_2437329 |title=Hearts 1914 Memorial Trust |publisher=Heart of Midlotian F.C. |work=Hearts News |date=31 August 2011 |access-date=9 October 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140514222033/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110831/hearts-1914-memorial-trust_2241384_2437329 |archive-date=14 May 2014 }}</ref> An annual pilgrimage is held by football supporters to Contalmaison every year,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/france-preparing-to-pay-respects-to-the-fallen-heroes-from-hearts-j92bp5ndsdb | title=France preparing to pay respects to the fallen heroes from Hearts |work=The Times  | date=10 November 2005 | access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110704/contalmaison-2011_2241384_2385896 |title=Contalmaison 2011 |publisher=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |work=Hearts News |date=4 July 2011 |access-date=9 October 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707021552/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110704/contalmaison-2011_2241384_2385896 |archive-date=7 July 2011 }}</ref> whilst Hearts hold their memorial services at Haymarket<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/hearts-team-that-will-never-be-forgotten-fjq37qrsf9p | title=Hearts team that will never be forgotten |work=The Times  | date=8 November 2008 | access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref> or, whilst it was in storage, at [[Tynecastle Park]].<ref>{{cite web | url=http://sport.scotsman.com/heartofmidlothianfc/Remebrance-service-at-Tynecastle.5804238.jp | title=Remembrance service at Tynecastle | publisher=Scotsman Publications | work=Edinburgh Evening News | date=7 November 2009 | access-date=9 October 2011}}</ref>

=== Inter war years ===
Hearts collected no senior silverware in the inter war years. [[Tommy Walker (footballer, born 1915)|Tommy Walker]] joined the Hearts ground staff aged 16 in February 1932. As Scottish clubs could not then officially sign players until the age of 17, Walker played [[Scottish Junior Football Association|junior]] football for [[Linlithgow Rose F.C.|Linlithgow Rose]] until his birthday in May.<ref>Speed et al., P78</ref> A talented and elegant inside-forward, Walker quickly earned a place in the Hearts first team, helping the side to victory in the 1933 Jubilee edition of the [[Rosebery Charity Cup]], in a season in which they finished 3rd in the league. He was a regular first team player by [[1933–34 in Scottish football|1933–34]] but despite some emphatic victories, inconsistent form limited Hearts to a sixth-place finish.

Despite Walker scoring 192 league goals for Hearts and playing in sides boasting numerous internationals, such as Scots [[David McCulloch|Dave McCulloch]], [[Barney Battles Jr.|Barney Battles]], [[Andrew Anderson (footballer)|Andy Anderson]] and [[Alex Massie (footballer)|Alex Massie]], [[Wales|Welshman]] Freddie Warren and Irishman Willie Reid, Walker was destined not to win a major honour as a player at [[Tynecastle Park|Tynecastle]]. The closest Hearts came to success during his period there was a second place league finish in [[1937–38 in Scottish football|1937–38]].

=== Tommy Walker's managerial era ===
The first seeds of the Tommy Walker managerial success at Hearts were sown by [[David McLean (footballer, born 1884)|Davie McLean]]. On 9 October 1948 after a mediocre start to the [[1948–49 in Scottish football|1948–49 season]], Hearts' manager McLean gave a competitive first team debut to 20 year old<ref name="bauld">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/players/bauldwillie.html|title=Willie Bauld - Hearts Career - from 01 May 1948 to 03 Mar 1962|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-date=26 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180126122724/http://londonhearts.com/scores/players/bauldwillie.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> centre forward [[Willie Bauld]]<ref name="hearts4849">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/sea/1948-49.html|title=1948-49|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> and 19 year old inside left [[Jimmy Wardhaugh]],<ref name="wardhaugh">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/players/wardhaughjimmy.html|title=Jimmy Wardhaugh - Hearts Career - from 21 Aug 1946 to 31 Oct 1960|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-date=26 January 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180126121851/http://londonhearts.com/scores/players/wardhaughjimmy.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> and 22 year old inside right [[Alfie Conn Sr.]]<ref name="conn">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/players/connalfie.html|title=Alfie Conn Snr - Hearts Career - from 14 Oct 1944 to 21 Apr 1945|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-date=27 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180727212223/http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/players/connalfie.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> had already broken through to the first team so this game marked the first time all three were deployed as a combined attacking force.<ref name="lh19481009">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/194810091.html|title=1948-10-09 Sat Hearts 6 East Fife 1|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> They became dubbed the ''Terrible Trio'' and scored over 900 Hearts goals between them<ref name=connobit>{{cite web|url=http://announce.jpress.co.uk/scotsman-publications/obituary/alfie-conn/1600260|title=Alfie Conn: Obituary|website=Announce.jpress.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161030081139/http://announce.jpress.co.uk/scotsman-publications/obituary/alfie-conn/1600260|archive-date=30 October 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> (Wardhaugh 376, Bauld 355, Conn 221).<ref name = hall>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/pages/HallOfFame|title=Heart of Midlothian - Hall of Fame|website=Heartsfc.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-date=4 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161204053409/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/pages/HallOfFame|url-status=dead}}</ref> As a unit they played 242 games together.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/alfie-conn-snr-last-surviving-member-of-hearts-terrible-trio-1513379.html|title=Alfie Conn Snr: Last surviving member of Hearts' 'Terrible Trio'|website=Independent.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018|date=23 January 2009|archive-date=29 December 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201229202445/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/alfie-conn-snr-last-surviving-member-hearts-terrible-trio-1513379.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> The combination of Wardhaugh's dribbling skills and non-stop running, Bauld's cerebral play and prodigious aerial ability, and Conn's energetic, tenacious style and powerful shooting complemented each other well.<ref name="style">Scott, ''The Terrible Trio'', 101–103</ref> Their first match as a forward combination ended in a 6–1 defeat of [[Scot Symon]]'s [[East Fife F.C.|East Fife]] team of the era.<ref name=hist44-54>[http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20080408/1944-1954_2241543_1283899 Hearts History 1944 – 54 www.heartsfc.co.uk] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170827003224/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20080408/1944-1954_2241543_1283899 |date=27 August 2017 }}</ref> This was notable as Symon's team had defeated the ''Maroons'' 4–0 three weeks earlier.<ref name = lh1948-09-18>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/194809181.html|title=1948-09-18 Sat East Fife 4 Hearts 0|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref>

A few weeks later in December 1948 Tommy Walker left during his third season at Chelsea to return to Hearts. He took the role of player-assistant to manager McLean. McLean's intention was that Walker would be a steadying influence in a developing young team. However, after a single appearance at right-half in a 1–0 home defeat by [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]], Walker retired to concentrate fully on learning the managerial ropes.<ref>Price, P10</ref> Tangible progress was made in the League Championship in 1949–50 when Hearts finished third. As Tommy Walker had become more influential, McLean was co-opted to the Board on 16 March 1950.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110214/david-mclean-remembered_2241384_2293245|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110217131453/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20110214/david-mclean-remembered_2241384_2293245|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 February 2011|title=David McLean remembered - Hearts News - Hearts News - News - Hearts - Hearts|date=17 February 2011|website=Heartsfc.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref><ref name = hist44-54/><ref name = hall/>

[[File:Heart of Midlothian FC League Performance.svg|300px|thumb|right|Chart of Hearts' yearly table positions in the League.]]McLean's death on 14 February 1951 saw Walker promoted to the position of manager. Walker's reign was to prove the most successful period in the club's history.<ref>Price, P12</ref> Walker was always quick to acknowledge the contribution made by McLean and his fatherly interest in the welfare and development of the players. The important foundations Walker inherited from McLean included the ''Terrible Trio'' forwards, the full back pair of [[Bobby Parker (footballer, born 1925)|Bobby Parker]] and [[Tam McKenzie]] and half backs [[Bobby Dougan]] and [[Davie Laing]]. To this established core [[John Cumming (Scottish footballer)|John Cumming]] had recently broken through to the first team in the left half position he was to dominate for many years. [[Freddie Glidden]] was already at Tynecastle but yet to first team debut as was the then schoolboy [[Dave Mackay]]. Walker made Parker the team captain.<ref name = hist44-54/><ref name = hall/>

Mackay's key signing as a professional was under Walker in 1952 (initially part-time whilst also working as a joiner). Mackay's pairing with Cumming at wing half was to become the nucleus of the team in the middle of the pitch. Mackay was a supremely talented all round player of ferocious tackling, endless running and sublime ball control. Cumming's ''Iron Man'' nickname says much of his fearless determination. Despite his commitment he retained control of his temper and was never booked in his career. Cumming was the only player to collect medals for all seven of the trophies Hearts won under Walker. "He never had a bad game. It was either a fairly good game or an excellent game," said Mackay later of his former teammate.<ref name=cummingobit>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2008/dec/16/john-cumming-obituary|title=Obituary: John Cumming|first=Ewan|last=Murray|date=16 December 2008|website=The Guardian|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> Both went on to become full Scotland internationalists while playing for Hearts.<ref name = hist44-54/><ref name = hall/>

Bauld's value to the team was underlined in 1952–53, when he missed eight vital league games through ankle injuries. Hearts were struggling, but with Bauld's return to full fitness came a change in fortunes. From the bottom half of the league they surged up the table to finish in fourth place (as they had the two previous seasons). That resurgence also took them to a [[1952–53 Scottish Cup]] semi final against Rangers before 116,262 fans at Hampden Park in Glasgow. Wardhaugh scored in the 2–1 defeat. Hearts were now though on an upward trajectory.<ref name = hist44-54/><ref name = hall/>

In [[1953–54 in Scottish football|1953–54]], Wardhaugh became the [[Scottish Football League|A Division]]'s top scorer with 27 goals as Hearts appeared set to win the [[Scottish football champions|League championship]]. However, on 13 March 1954 in the Scottish Cup quarter final 3–0 defeat away to Aberdeen, Parker broke his jaw, Conn injured his back, and Wardhaugh collected a serious shin bone injury. Dougan already had a lengthy knee injury meaning 9 November 1953 was his last competitive Hearts first team game (Dougan only subsequently played for Hearts in friendlies). Walker immediately tried Glidden to cover and he took over the centre half berth from Dougan. A stuttering end to their season saw [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] overtake them.<ref name=bauldbio2>{{cite web|url=http://www.williebauldmc.co.uk/html/biograph2.html|title=Biograph2|website=Williebauldmc.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> The young Mackay was given his first team debut on 7 November of that 1953–54 season one week before his nineteenth birthday. Naturally more left sided than right, Mackay played in the number six jersey normally associated with the absent Cumming. Mackay's next two appearances though weren't until mid March immediately after the Aberdeen cup defeat when again he played in Cumming's position. It wasn't until 17 April 1954 in a 1–0 win at Clyde that Walker first selected Mackay, Glidden and Cumming in the numbers four, five and six.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195404171.html#team|title=1954-04-17 Sat Clyde 0 Hearts 1|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref><ref name = hist44-54/><ref name = hall/>

The team was boosted by the signing of [[Ian Crawford (footballer)|Ian Crawford]] in August 1954. Mackay was given his extended place in the team in the 1954–55 season immediately after Laing's 5 September transfer to Clyde. It was from this point that Walker settled on Mackay, Glidden and Cumming as his combination for the number four, five and six jerseys.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195409111.html|title=1954-09-11 Sat Hearts 5 Partick Thistle 4|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> They promptly became a trophy winning force lifting the first of seven trophies over nine seasons between 1954 and 1963. In October of the [[1954–55 in Scottish football|1954–55]] season they won their first trophy since 1906, 48 years before. They beat [[Motherwell F.C.|Motherwell]] 4–2 in the [[1954 Scottish League Cup final]]. Bauld scored three and Wardhaugh scored one in the final giving the team their break through trophy. Hearts gained some recompense against Celtic from the season before by beating them home and away in that [[1954–55 Scottish League Cup]] group stage.<ref name=hist54-64>http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20080802/1954-1964_2241543_1356683 {{dead link|date=March 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name = hall/>

After signing [[Alex Young (footballer, born 1937)|Alex Young]] and [[Bobby Kirk (footballer)|Bobby Kirk]], Walker's side proceeded to win the [[1955–56 Scottish Cup]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QKKqENumvuY| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/QKKqENumvuY| archive-date=30 October 2021|title=Scottish F.A. Cup Final - Hearts Beat Celtic 3-1 (1956)|last=British Pathé|date=13 April 2014|access-date=27 July 2018|publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> They thrashed Rangers 4–0 in the quarter-finals with goals from Crawford, Conn and a Bauld double.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195603031.html|title=1956-03-03 Sat Hearts 4 Rangers 0|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> Cumming's commitment to the team was typified in that [[1956 Scottish Cup final]] before 132,840 fans. With blood streaming from a first half head injury from a clash with Celtic's [[Willie Fernie (footballer)|Willie Fernie]] he said, "Blood doesn't show on a maroon jersey". He returned to the playing field in the 3–1 win and was man of the match. That quote is now displayed above the entrance to the players tunnel at [[Tynecastle Park|Tynecastle]]. Kirk could play in either full back role<ref name="kirkobit">{{cite web|url=http://www.scotsman.com/news/obituaries/bobby-kirk-1-788895|title=Bobby Kirk|website=Scotsman.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> and played on the right in the final at the expense of Parker. Glidden lifted the trophy as Hearts captain in what he recalled as the "sweetest" moment in his footballing career.<ref name="Memories">{{cite book | last = Robertson | first = Rob|author2=Kiddie, Paul | title = Hearts: Great Tynecastle Tales| publisher = Mainstream | year = 2005 |page=186| id = () | isbn = 1-84596-003-3}}</ref><ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

Wardhaugh was the top tier's leading scorer again that season. The scorers in the cup final win over Celtic were Crawford with two and one from Conn. Conn ended that 1955–56 season at the peak of his powers aged 29 with a career best 29 goals from 41 games. On 2 May 1956 two weeks after the cup win Conn became the third of the terrible trio to collect a full [[Scotland men's national football team|Scotland]] cap. At Hampden Park he put his side ahead after 12 minutes in a 1–1 draw with [[Austria national football team|Austria]]. However the following September he suffered a broken jaw playing against Hibernian keeping him out until January.<ref name=alfieobit>[http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20090107/alfie-conn_2241384_1511597 Hearts FC Alfie Conn obituary] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161030220435/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20090107/alfie-conn_2241384_1511597 |date=30 October 2016 }}</ref><ref name = "telegraph obit">{{cite news |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/hearts/4163851/Hearts-legend-Alfie-Conn-senior-dies-aged-82.html |first=Andrew |last=Lomax |access-date=1 April 2013 |date=7 January 2009 |title=Hearts legend Alfie Conn senior dies aged 82 |work=Daily Telegraph |publisher=Telegraph Media Group}}</ref> The days of the ''Terrible Trio'' as a combined force were nearing their end.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

17 year old [[Gordon Marshall (footballer, born 1939)|Gordon Marshall]] debuted in 1956 as did [[George Thomson (footballer, born 1936)|George Thomson]] in February 1957. Marshall, a future England under-23 internationalist, became a Hearts goalkeeping regular until 1963. Hearts led the Scottish League for most of the 1956–57 season. The title hinged on Rangers visit to Tynecastle on 13 April. A capacity crowd watched a tense game in which Rangers keeper, [[George Niven]], was man of the match. Hearts could not beat him and the only goal came from [[Billy Simpson (footballer, born 1929)|Billy Simpson]] of Rangers who scored on the break in 35 minutes. Rangers had games in hand which they won to overtake Hearts and lift the trophy.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

Walker completed the set of having won all three major Scottish football trophies with the League Championship in [[1957–58 in Scottish football|1957–58]]. Conn suffered a serious ankle injury meaning he only played in five league games all season. Injury hit Conn left Hearts for [[Raith Rovers]] in September 1958 just two years after his 1956 zenith. He did so after 408 first team games and 221 goals.<ref name = hall/> With an injury hit Bauld only playing nine times in the league title win a new Hearts attacking trio were dominant. For a third time Wardhaugh was the League's top marksman with 28 strikes. This was one ahead of [[Jimmy Murray (footballer, born 1933)|Jimmy Murray]]'s 27 and four more than Young's 24. Mackay, now captain, was fourth in Hearts' league scoring charts with 12. Hearts won that [[Scottish football champions|League title]] in [[1957–58 in Scottish football|1957–58]] with record-breaking points, goals scored and goal difference. Their record from 34 league games of 62 points out of a maximum possible 68 was 13 more than their nearest rival. They scored 132 goals (still the Scottish top tier record) with only 29 against for a record net difference of +103. This was Hearts' greatest ever league side. Murray and Mackay both played for Scotland at the [[1958 FIFA World Cup]] where Murray scored in a 1–1 draw against Yugoslavia. Parker was a fringe player in the league winning season, his last season as a Hearts player. He moved to the club coaching staff before joining the Board of Directors where he also had a spell as chairman.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

In the [[1958–59 Scottish League Cup]] group stage Hearts eliminated Rangers. That October the [[1958 Scottish League Cup final]] was won with a heavy 5–1 defeat of [[Partick Thistle F.C.|Partick Thistle]]. Bauld and Murray each scored two and [[Johnny Hamilton (footballer, born 1935)|Johnny Hamilton]] netted one. Hearts defended their league title by being leaders in mid December. However a side visiting Ibrox missing injured Mackay were beaten 5–0 with all goals in the first 35 minutes. This put Rangers into top position in the table on goal average.<ref name="dec58">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195812131.html|title=1958-12-13 Sat Rangers 5 Hearts 0|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> This precipitated a run of only two wins from the next seven games without injured Mackay. Hearts beat Queen of the South in a 2–1 home league win on 7 March 1959.<ref name="lh19590307">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195903071.html|title=1959-03-07 Sat Hearts 2 Queen of the South 1|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> After that QoS game Rangers with six games to play were firm favourites for the title, six points ahead of second placed Hearts.<ref name="lh19590307"/> Even if Hearts were to win their remaining seven games including a game in hand and beating Rangers in their visit Tynecastle in Rangers' penultimate game of the season,<ref name="lh5859">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/sea/1958-59.html|title=1958-59|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> Rangers would still have to drop two points elsewhere and give away a superior goal average.<ref name="lh19590307"/> The league game against QoS was Mackay's last for Hearts after they accepted a bid of £32,000 from [[Tottenham Hotspur F.C.|Tottenham Hotspur]] for their captain who was fit at this time despite having had lengthy spells out injured in the previous 12 months. Bobby Rankin was brought in to bolster the squad and scored twice in each of his first two games (both victories). On the penultimate Saturday of the league campaign goals by Cumming and Rankin at home to Rangers<ref name="lhhttp://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195904111.html">{{cite web|url=https://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195904111.html|title=1959-04-11 Sat Hearts 2 Rangers 0|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref> meant Hearts were four points behind with a game in hand. In midweek they next won 4–2 at Aberdeen with Rankin scoring a hat-trick.<ref name="hl19590415">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195904151.html|title=1959-04-15 Wed Aberdeen 2 Hearts 4|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> The last day of the season began with Rangers two points clear with an identical goal average to Hearts. Rangers thus needed a point to clinch the title but lost 2–1 at home to Aberdeen. Despite missing Bobby Kirk at right back with a knee injury, Rankin's ninth goal from his fifth Hearts game had Hearts 1–0 up at half time at [[Celtic Park]]. Any victory would have given Hearts the title. Then Celtic's [[Bertie Auld]] playing at left wing equalised before [[Eric Smith (Scottish footballer)|Eric Smith]] scored Celtic's winning second goal to seal the title for their cross city rivals<ref name="lh19590418">{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/195904181.html|title=1959-04-18 Sat Celtic 2 Hearts 1|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> leaving those at Tynecastle to wonder what would have happened if Mackay hadn't been sold when he was.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

Mackay's name as a club mainstay at half back was eventually taken over by [[Billy Higgins (Scottish footballer)|Billy Higgins]]. That League Cup win was also Glidden's last trophy as a recurring back injury that season numbered his playing days at Tynecastle. 36 year old MacKenzie left in 1959 as did Wardhaugh. He scored 206 goals in 304 league games and a total of 376 goals in 518 games for Hearts.<ref name = hall/><ref name = hist54-64/>

After collecting three Scottish championships and 19 full Scotland caps at Hibernian, [[Gordon Smith (footballer, born 1924)|Gordon Smith]] had a recurring ankle injury leading to his [[free transfer (association football)|free transfer]] in 1959. Smith believed that an operation could cure the injury<ref name="montford">{{cite news |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/newspaper/archive/1964/0222/Pg004.html |title=Newspaper Archive |page=4  |date=22 February 1964 |newspaper=[[The Irish Times]] |issn=0791-5144 |location=Dublin |language=en-ie |access-date=18 April 2022}}</ref> and paid for an operation on the offending ankle himself. He then signed for Hearts, his boyhood heroes.<ref name = "montford"/> He enjoyed immediate success at [[Tynecastle Park|Tynecastle]], winning both the [[1959 Scottish League Cup final]] and league title in his [[1959–60 in Scottish football|first season]] with the club.<ref name = "montford"/> Hamilton scored for Hearts in that second successive League Cup Final and Young hit the winner. [[Third Lanark]] were beaten 2–1. 1960 ended with Walker being awarded the [[Order of the British Empire|OBE]] for services to football.<ref name="walkerobit">{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12626976.Tommy_Walker_dies_at_77/|title=Tommy Walker dies at 77|website=HeraldScotland|date=12 January 1993 |access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref><ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

The 1960s saw Hearts fortunes fluctuate as Walker attempted to adapt to football's tactical changes by implementing a 4–2–4 formation. Young and Thomson departed for [[Everton F.C.|Everton]] in November 1960. At Everton Young was known as ''The Golden Vision'' and became another from the Walker production line of full Scotland internationalists. Smith had an injury hit season leading to his joining Dundee (who became the third club with whom he won the Scottish title). Hearts signed further future full internationalists in [[Willie Wallace]] and [[David Holt (footballer, born 1936)|David Holt]]. Hearts lost the [[1961 Scottish League Cup final]] after a replay. Cumming scored a deserved equalising penalty for Hearts in the first game 1–1 draw they largely dominated against the Scot Symon managed Rangers. [[Norrie Davidson]] scored a then equalising Hearts goal when they lost in the 3–1 replay defeat.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

Bauld left Hearts in 1962 with 355 goals from 510 first team appearances.<ref name = hall/> Another future internationalist, [[Willie Hamilton (footballer, born 1938)|Willie Hamilton]], joined for the run culminating in the [[1962 Scottish League Cup final]] win. Hearts won the trophy for a fourth time with a 1–0 final win over [[Willie Waddell]]'s fine Kilmarnock side of that era. Davidson's goal this time proved decisive. Like in the 1954–55 win Hearts eliminated Celtic in that [[1962–63 Scottish League Cup]] group stage.<ref name = hist54-64/><ref name = hall/>

In [[1964–65 Scottish Division One|1964–65]] Hearts fought out a championship title race with Waddell's Kilmarnock. In the era of two points for a win Hearts were three points clear with two games remaining. Hearts drew with Dundee United meaning the last game of the season with the two title challengers playing each other at Tynecastle would be a league decider. Kilmarnock needed to win by a two-goal margin to take the title. Hearts entered the game as favourites with both a statistical and home advantage. They also had a solid pedigree of trophy winning under Walker. Waddell's Kilmarnock in contrast had been nearly men. Four times in the previous five seasons they had finished league runners-up including Hearts’ triumph in 1960. Killie had also lost three domestic cup finals during the same period including the 1962 League Cup Final defeat to Hearts. Hearts had won five of the six senior cup finals they played in under Walker. Even the final they had lost was in a replay after drawing the first game. Hearts' [[Roald Jensen]] hit the post after six minutes. Kilmarnock then scored twice through [[Davie Sneddon]] and Brian McIlroy after 27 and 29 minutes. [[Alan Gordon (Scottish footballer)|Alan Gordon]] had an excellent chance to clinch the title for Hearts in second half injury time but was denied by a [[Bobby Ferguson (footballer, born 1945)|Bobby Ferguson]] diving save pushing the ball past the post. The 2–0 defeat meant Hearts lost the title by an average of 0.042 goals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://footballpink.net/2013/09/22/killies-final-day-victory-breaks-hearts/|title=Killie's final day victory breaks Hearts|date=22 September 2013|website=Footballpink.net|access-date=27 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161030142924/https://footballpink.net/2013/09/22/killies-final-day-victory-breaks-hearts/|archive-date=30 October 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.londonhearts.com/scores/games/196504241.html|title=1965-04-24 Sat Hearts 0 Kilmarnock 2|website=Londonhearts.com|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-93_7Gz5FTQ| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/-93_7Gz5FTQ| archive-date=30 October 2021|title=Hearts 0 Killie 2 (24/04/1965)|date=10 July 2008|access-date=27 July 2018|publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Subsequently, Hearts were instrumental in pushing through a change to use goal difference to separate teams level on points. Ironically this rule change later denied Hearts the title in 1985–86.<ref name=hist64-74>[http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20061108/1964-1974_2241543_1458271 Hearts History 1964 – 74 www.heartsfc.co.uk] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160521154848/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk.p.preprod.performgroup.com/articles/20061108/1964-1974_2241543_1458271 |date=21 May 2016 }}</ref><ref name = hall/>

Following a slump in results, Walker resigned in September 1966. Under his management Hearts had won 7 senior trophies and been runners up in five others. Cumming left the playing staff a year later and joined the coaching team.<ref name = hist64-74/><ref name = hall/>

=== Later 20th century ===
The highlight of the late 60s was the run to the 1968 Scottish Cup Final when they lost 3–1 to [[George Farm]]'s [[Dunfermline Athletic]]. The players of greatest note in the late sixties were [[Jim Cruickshank]], [[Alan Anderson (footballer)|Alan Anderson]] and [[Donald Ford]] with [[Drew Busby]] joining the three in the 1970s. The high point of the 1970s was another run to the Scottish Cup Final. In 1975–76 they again lost 3–1 in the final this time to Rangers. After the advent of the ten team Premier Division in 1975, Hearts were subsequently relegated for the first time in [[1976–77 in Scottish football|1977]]. This began a sequence of [[yo-yo club|yo-yoing]] between the Premier League and First Division six times in seven seasons.

On 25 May 1981, 34-year-old [[Wallace Mercer]] became chairman after buying a controlling interest in Hearts for £265,000.<ref name =mercer>{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/news/12442782.Wallace_Mercer_Businessman_and_former_chairman_of_Hearts_FC/|title=Wallace Mercer Businessman and former chairman of Hearts FC|website=HeraldScotland|date=18 January 2006 |access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref> Hearts had just been relegated from the top flight for the third time in five seasons. The following December (1981), Mercer promoted [[Alex MacDonald (footballer, born 1948)|Alex MacDonald]] to be player-manager. At the end of the 1982–83 season, Hearts were promoted back to the top flight. This marked an upturn in their fortunes to rejoin the more competitive clubs in Scotland's top flight. The [[1985–86 in Scottish football|1985–86 season]] was their best since 1965. The league campaign started with the loss of five of the first eight games. From there the club went on a 27-game unbeaten league run, reaching the top of the league on 21 December after a 1–0 win at St Mirren.

Hearts needed a draw from the last game of the season away to [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] on 3 May 1986 to win the Scottish league title. Before that final game they were two points ahead of Celtic and with a superior goal difference of four goals. However, this strong statistical position was undermined in the run up to the game when several players in the Hearts squad were hit by a viral infection. [[Craig Levein]] failed to recover to make the game in Dundee.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/football/teams/hearts/5363880/What-a-heartbreaker-How-Hearts-lost-the-Scottish-title-to-Celtic-in-1986.html|title=How Hearts lost the Scottish title to Celtic in 1986|first=Roddy|last=Forsyth|date=22 May 2009|access-date=27 July 2018|website=Telegraph.co.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6ZFezYotlVk#t=380.218895| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/6ZFezYotlVk| archive-date=30 October 2021|title=That was The Team That Was Part2|last=Subtitledvideos4|date=20 December 2010|access-date=27 July 2018|publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Celtic were 4–0 up away at St Mirren at half time in their final fixture. Thus, at half time the players knew that they would have to deliver a result at [[Dens Park]]. Substitute [[Albert Kidd]] forced Hearts to concede a corner kick with seven minutes remaining. The in-swinging corner was touched on and fell to Kidd who put Dundee ahead. This was the first goal Hearts had conceded from a corner all season. Hearts now needed an equaliser to win the title. However, Kidd went on a run with the ball from the halfway line down the right wing beating two Hearts players. After then playing a one-two with a teammate on the edge of the Hearts box he finished to score a second with four minutes left. Dundee won 2–0.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UCjEsN4E85s| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211030/UCjEsN4E85s| archive-date=30 October 2021|title=Dundee V Hearts 1986 Albert Kidd|last=DeeLicious|date=19 March 2007|access-date=27 July 2018|publisher=YouTube}}{{cbignore}}</ref> This combined with Celtic winning 5–0 against St Mirren meant the top two clubs finished the season on the same number of points. Hearts lost out to Celtic by a goal difference of three. Had goal difference been the rule in 1965 Hearts would have been champions; had goal average still applied in 1986, they would have won the league. Hearts lobbying after the league loss in 1965 cost them the title in 1986.

Hearts had been chasing a League and Scottish Cup double. After eliminating Rangers and [[Jim McLean]]'s Dundee United they faced [[Alex Ferguson]]'s Aberdeen in the final; Aberdeen [[1986 Scottish Cup final|won 3–0]] meaning Hearts finished runners-up as they had in the league.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/that-1980s-sports-blog/2015/may/01/albert-kidd-day-hearts-dundee-hibs-celtic-1986|title=How Albert Kidd became a Hibs and Celtic legend without playing for them|first=Steven|last=Pye|date=1 May 2015|website=The Guardian|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref>

Hearts finished league runners-up again in [[1987–88 Scottish Premier Division|1988]] and [[1991–92 Scottish Premier Division|1992]]. The club reached the quarter-finals of the [[1988–89 UEFA Cup]] losing out to [[FC Bayern Munich|Bayern Munich]] 2–1 on aggregate. After MacDonald's summer 1990 departure the club struggled to settle on a manager. Within a two-year period, [[Joe Jordan]], [[Sandy Clark]] and [[Tommy McLean]] were all sacked. From April 1989 to April 1994, Hearts went on a run of 22 games in a row without defeat against arch-rivals Hibernian in the [[Edinburgh derby]].

In 1994 Mercer sold his shares in Hearts to Chris Robinson and Leslie Deans. Under Mercer, Hearts finished second in the Scottish top tier three times and once in the Scottish Cup, but his time at the helm concluded without senior silverware. His personal influence at the club is perhaps best remembered with [[History of Hibernian F.C.#Takeover bid by Hearts (1989–1991)|an attempted merger with Hibs in 1990]]. Seen by Hibs fans as an attempted take over to liquidate their club, Mercer's attempts were met with bitterness and acrimony before he backed away.<ref name =mercer/><ref name=saviours>[https://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/hibs/creative-accountancy-how-jim-mclean-and-others-were-unlikely-saviours-hibs-wallace-mercer-circled-2873914 'Creative accountancy': How Jim McLean - and others - were unlikely saviours of Hibs as Wallace Mercer circled], ''[[The Scotsman]]'', 4 June 2020</ref>

In [[1997–98 in Scottish football|1998]], Hearts beat Rangers [[1998 Scottish Cup final|2–1]] to lift the Scottish Cup under the management of ex Hearts player, [[Jim Jefferies (footballer)|Jim Jefferies]]. [[Colin Cameron (footballer)|Colin Cameron]] scored a first-minute penalty and [[Stéphane Adam]] added after half time. This was Hearts' first senior trophy win since the [[1962–63 Scottish League Cup]] won in the Tommy Walker era.

=== Into the 21st century ===
Hearts finished third in 2003 and 2004, and reached the inaugural group stages of the [[UEFA Cup]] in 2004–05, but finished bottom of their group, despite [[Robbie Neilson]]'s goal giving a 2–1 victory over [[FC Basel]]. During the 2004–05 season, they finished fifth in the league.

In 2004, then club CEO Chris Robinson announced plans to sell Tynecastle, which he claimed was "not fit for purpose", and instead have Hearts rent [[Murrayfield Stadium|Murrayfield]] from the [[Scottish Rugby Union]].<ref>[http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/sport.cfm?id=1455932004 Tynecastle architect says £100,000 to fix stadium], ''[[The Scotsman]]''. {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051110132123/http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/sport.cfm?id=1455932004 |date=10 November 2005 }}</ref> This move was deemed necessary due to the club's increasingly large debt. The plan was very unpopular with supporters, and a campaign, entitled ''Save Our Hearts'', was set up to try to block the move.<ref>[http://quicksitebuilder.cnet.com/bonnjoy/thefederationofheartssupportersclubs/id11.html Save our Hearts] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060216234818/http://quicksitebuilder.cnet.com/bonnjoy/thefederationofheartssupportersclubs/id11.html |date=16 February 2006 }}</ref> As Robinson and his supporters had a slight majority of the club's shares, a preliminary deal to sell the stadium was struck with the Cala property development company for just over £20 million.<ref>[http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/sport.cfm?id=1073472004 Tynecastle sale to go through, but at what price?] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071022073805/http://thescotsman.scotsman.com/sport.cfm?id=1073472004 |date=22 October 2007 }}, ''The Scotsman''.</ref>

In early June 2013, during the close season, a Hearts media statement stated that they would need to raise £500,000 in capital to keep the club up and running during the break between seasons. On 17 June 2013, Heart of Midlothian began the process of entering into [[administration (law)|administration]] with debts of £25 million, owing recently bankrupt [[Ūkio bankas]] £15 million.<ref>{{cite news |title=Hearts: SPL side to enter administration |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/22944291 |access-date=29 August 2013}}</ref>

On 18 June 2013, a Scandinavian consortium offered to pay the club £500,000 immediately in return for a share of any future transfer income from up to 12 players; this was rejected by Hearts. The process of entering administration began on 19 June 2013 when the club's parent company, Ukio Bankas Investment Group (UBIG), filed papers at the Court of Session on Edinburgh for accountancy firm [[BDO Global|BDO]] to be named as administrators.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/22963110 Hearts rejected investment offer before administration application], BBC Sport, 18 June 2013</ref><ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/22953448 Hearts placed into administration and deducted 15 points], BBC Sport, 19 June 2013</ref>

===Administration===
On 17 June 2013 Hearts announced that they had lodged court papers stating their intention to enter administration, and on 19 June 2013 the administrators BDO were appointed to run the club.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/sport/football/bdo-appointed-to-run-hearts-in-administration.1371649500|title=BDO appointed to run Hearts in administration|work=Herald Scotland|date=19 June 2013 }}</ref> This meant that the club was unable to register players over 21 until February 2014 at the earliest. As long as they were still in administration they would not be able to bring in players of any age.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/23536242|title=Hearts: Registration ban to run until February 2014|newspaper=BBC Sport|date=August 2013}}</ref>

As well as the signing embargo, Hearts were to be deducted a third of the previous season's points tally which meant the club would start the 2013–2014 season with −15 points. During this period the BDO administrator Trevor Birch pleaded with Hearts fans to purchase season tickets and stated that they needed to sell at least another 3,000 season tickets to raise another £800,000 to keep the club running and avoiding liquidation. The fans met this number and took total season ticket sales beyond the 10,000 mark, giving the club more survival time.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20130712/season-ticket-update_2241384_3232942|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130826171529/http://www.heartsfc.co.uk/articles/20130712/season-ticket-update_2241384_3232942|url-status=dead|title=Season ticket update – Hearts<!-- Bot generated title -->|archive-date=26 August 2013|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref>
A deadline of 12 July 2013 was set for interested parties to put in formal bids for the club;<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.heraldscotland.com/sport/football/hearts-administrators-set-bid-deadline-for-club.1372350075|title=Hearts administrators set bid deadline for club|work=Herald Scotland|date=27 June 2013 }}</ref> there were three bids entered for the club which were received from the supporters group "The Foundation of Hearts",<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scotsman.com/news/foundation-of-hearts-submits-offer-1-2999263|title=Foundation of Hearts submits offer|website=Scotsman.com}}</ref> the second from a new company called "HMFC limited" which was backed by American firm Club Sports 9 and a third from former Livingston FC owner [[Angelo Massone]] through Five Star Football Limited.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scotsman.com/sport/football/latest/hearts-administration-three-bids-in-for-club-1-3000487|title=Hearts administration: Three bids in for club|website=Scotsman.com}}</ref>

On 15 August 2013, The Foundation of Hearts were given preferred bidders status to make a CVA with Hearts' creditors. The money that the foundation used to purchase the club came from monthly donations from fans; the foundation received an interest-free loan from a wealthy fan, which was to be paid back using the monthly direct debts from the fans.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.express.co.uk/sport/football/426157/Foundation-of-Hearts-direct-greatest-fan-drive|title=Foundation of Hearts direct 'greatest' fan drive|author=David Ewart|work=Express.co.uk|date=September 2013}}</ref> On 2 December, Hearts' creditors agreed to the CVA deal proposed by The Foundation of Hearts.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.insolvencynews.com/article/16298/corporate/hearts-cva-agreed-by-creditors|title=Hearts CVA agreed by creditors|website=Insolvencynews.com}}</ref>

The club's relegation from the [[Scottish Premiership]] was confirmed on 5 April 2014.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/26796705 | title=Hearts' relegation from the Scottish Premiership was confirmed despite victory against Partick Thistle. | publisher=[[BBC Sport]] | work=bbc.co.uk/sport | date=5 April 2014 | access-date=6 April 2014}}</ref> Hearts won 4–2 away to [[Partick Thistle F.C.|Partick Thistle]], but [[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] beat [[Motherwell F.C.|Motherwell]] 3–2, making it impossible for Hearts to catch up.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eurosport.com/football/scottish-premier-league/2013-2014/hearts-relegated-despite-victory_sto4202415/story.shtml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191226203445/https://www.eurosport.com/football/scottish-premier-league/2013-2014/hearts-relegated-despite-victory_sto4202415/story.shtml|url-status=dead|archive-date=26 December 2019|title=Hearts relegated despite victory|date=5 April 2014|website=Eurosport.xom|access-date=2 November 2021}}</ref>

On Monday 12 May 2014, the [[Ann Budge]]-fronted Bidco 1874 took control of Heart of Midlothian Plc, thus bringing to an end to Vladimir Romanov's involvement with the club. Budge, became an unpaid executive chairwoman of the club. The Bidco group planned to hold the club for a possible five years, before the fan-backed Foundation of Hearts supporters group would take control. The foundation put in £1 million for the running of the club until the final legal exit of administration. The foundation then paid a further £2.6 million (£2.5m to cover the loan given by Bidco1874 Ltd to Hearts to finance the Creditors' Voluntary Agreement + £100,000 for the shares) to take 75% of the shares in the club, and with that the running and decision making within the club. In addition, the Foundation also committed itself to provide a further £2.8m (£1.4m per year for two years) working capital for the club. Funding for the deal came from 8,000+ people donating cash via a monthly direct debit.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/27347133|title=Hearts: Ann Budge to start at Tynecastle on Monday|newspaper=BBC Sport|date=9 May 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.foundationofhearts.org/faqs/|title=Foundation of Hearts|website=Bbc.co.uk|access-date=5 June 2014|archive-date=31 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140531090820/http://www.foundationofhearts.org/faqs/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The club officially exited [[Administration (law)|administration]] on 11 June 2014, also bringing to an end the signing embargo that had been imposed upon the club a year earlier.<ref>{{cite news|last=McLauchlin|first=Brian|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/27794267|title=Hearts: Club exit administration, signing ban lifted|access-date=3 April 2018|work=BBC Sport|date=11 June 2014}}</ref>

=== Post-administration ===
Hearts earned an immediate return to the [[Scottish Premiership]] by clinching the [[2014–15 Scottish Championship]] title with seven games remaining.<ref>[http://www.scotzine.com/2015/03/hearts-crowned-spfl-championship-title-winners/ Hearts have been SPFL Championship title winners] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150521031717/http://www.scotzine.com/2015/03/hearts-crowned-spfl-championship-title-winners/ |date=21 May 2015 }} Scotzine. 22 March 2015. Retrieved 18 May 2015.</ref> Hearts remained undefeated for the first 20 league matches before a 3–2 home defeat to [[Falkirk F.C.|Falkirk]] ended that run.<ref>[http://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hearts/hearts-2-falkirk-3-unbeaten-run-over-for-jambos-1-3670211 Hearts 2–3 Falkirk: Jambos Unbeaten Run Ends] Edinburgh Evening News. 24 January 2015. Retrieved 18 May 2015.</ref> They won the title by winning 29 of 36 games, scoring 96 goals and conceding just 26, with a points total of 91.<ref>{{cite web |title=Scottish Premiership Table 2019/20 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/scottish-premiership/table |website=BBC.co.uk |access-date=21 May 2020}}</ref> They finished the season 21 points ahead of their city rivals and nearest challengers [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]] and 24 points ahead of third-placed [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]]. The season included handing [[Cowdenbeath F.C.|Cowdenbeath]] a joint-club record 10–0 defeat.<ref>[https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/31563172 Heart of Midlothian 10–0 Cowdenbeath] BBC Sport. 28 February 2015. Retrieved 18 May 2015.</ref> At the [[Professional Footballers' Association Scotland|PFA Scotland]] Awards, Hearts had six players named in [[PFA Scotland Team of the Year#Championship 2|Championship Team of the Year]],<ref>[http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-scotland-announce-teams-of-the-year/ PFA Scotland Teams of the Year 2014–15] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518110322/http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-scotland-announce-teams-of-the-year/ |date=18 May 2015 }} PFA Scotland. 1 May 2015. Retrieved 19 May 2015.</ref> two [[PFA Scotland Young Player of the Year|Young Player of the Year]] nominees,<ref>[http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-scotland-player-of-the-year-nominees/ PFA Scotland Young Player of the Year 2014–15 nominees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150519155702/http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-scotland-player-of-the-year-nominees/ |date=19 May 2015 }} PFA Scotland. 24 April 2015. Retrieved 19 May 2015.</ref> and three Championship Player of the Year nominees,<ref>[http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-announce-player-of-the-year-nominees/ PFA Scotland Player of the Year 2014–15 nominees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150520141126/http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/pfa-announce-player-of-the-year-nominees/ |date=20 May 2015 }} PFA Scotland. 21 April 2015. Retrieved 19 May 2015.</ref> while [[Robbie Neilson]] was shortlisted for [[PFA Scotland Manager of the Year|Manager of the Year]].<ref>[http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/gordon-strachan-announces-pfas-manager-of-year-nominees/ PFA Scotland Manager of the Year 2014–15 nominees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518123741/http://pfascotland.co.uk/2015/news/gordon-strachan-announces-pfas-manager-of-year-nominees/ |date=18 May 2015 }} PFA Scotland. 30 April 2015. Retrieved 19 May 2015.</ref>

This period of renewed stability unravelled in the years following 2015. Despite finishing as runners-up in the [[2019 Scottish Cup final]], the club could only achieve mid-table placings in [[2016–17 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2017]], [[2017–18 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2018]] and [[2018–19 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2019]]. This decline took a turn for the worse in [[2019–20 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2019–20]] as Hearts were relegated after finishing bottom of the [[Scottish Premiership]], having won only four matches across the course of the season which had been truncated due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Celtic champions & Hearts relegated after SPFL ends season |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/52646282 |access-date=21 May 2020}}</ref> Their relegation was confirmed in June 2020, after league reconstruction talks instigated by Budge collapsed. The club confirmed that they would be pursuing legal action against the SPFL following their demotion to the [[Scottish Championship]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Hearts to mount legal challenge over Scottish Premiership relegation |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53053246 |access-date=17 June 2020}}</ref> The legal action failed, as a [[Scottish Football Association]] arbitration panel ruled that the SPFL had acted within its powers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53526063 |title=Hearts & Partick Thistle relegations confirmed by arbitration panel |website=BBC Sport |publisher=BBC |date=27 July 2020 |access-date=27 July 2020}}</ref>

Robbie Neilson was appointed as Hearts manager for a second time in June 2020, signing a three-year deal after leaving [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]], who had recently been promoted to the Scottish Premiership.<ref>{{cite news |title=Robbie Neilson: Hearts name Dundee Utd boss to replace Daniel Stendel |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53131136 |access-date=22 June 2020}}</ref> Former manager [[Jim Jefferies (footballer)|Jim Jefferies]] was recruited as an advisor to the board and manager in July.<ref>{{cite news |title=Jim Jefferies: Ex-Hearts boss returns as sporting director search halted |work=BBC Sport |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/53415655 |access-date=16 July 2020}}</ref> In August 2020, Andrew McKinlay was appointed as the club's new Chief Executive.<ref>{{cite web|title=Chairman's Statement {{!}} Heart Of Midlothian Football Club|url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/news/article/chairmans-statement-1-2-3-4|access-date=17 August 2020|website=Heartsfc.co.uk}}</ref> In June 2021, club captain Steven Naismith announced his retirement from football, taking up the role of Football Development Manager, focusing on the development of youth players "making their way towards the first team".<ref>{{cite web|title=Naismith retires and takes up new role {{!}} Heart Of Midlothian Football Club|url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/news/article/naismith-retires-and-takes-up-new-role|access-date=16 June 2021|website=Heartsfc.co.uk}}</ref>

On 30 August 2021, Hearts chairwoman Ann Budge officially transferred the club's shares to the Foundation of Hearts, meaning Hearts officially became the biggest fan-owned club in the United Kingdom.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hearts/hearts-fans-will-officially-own-their-club-today-as-foh-shares-transfer-is-completed-3363793/|title= Hearts fans will officially own their club TODAY as FoH shares transfer is completed|access-date=30 August 2021|work=Edinburgh Evening News}}</ref>

Hearts won the [[2020–21 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2020–21]] Scottish Championship, finishing ahead of second-placed [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] by 12 points<ref>{{cite web | url=https://spfl.co.uk/news/hearts-clinch-championship-title | title=Hearts clinch Championship title | SPFL }}</ref> and confirming their return to the Scottish Premiership. In their first [[2021–22 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|season]] back in the top flight, Hearts finished third and secured European group stage football in the [[UEFA Conference League]]. [[2022–23 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|The following season]], Hearts secured a fourth-placed finish. After finishing third in the [[2023–24 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2023–24 season]] they returned to European football; initially entering the [[UEFA Europa League]] final play-off stage, however, they failed to advance and dropped into the UEFA Conference League [[UEFA Conference League#Group stage and knockout phase|league stage]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Barry |date=5 May 2024 |title=Hearts secure third place: European info and dates with £5m UEFA income guaranteed |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hearts/hearts-secure-third-place-european-info-and-dates-with-ps5m-uefa-income-guaranteed-4616982 |access-date=29 July 2024 |website=Edinburgh Evening News}}</ref> After gaining a single point in their first six league games of the [[2024–25 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2024–25 season]] (the worst start to a season in the club's history), manager [[Steven Naismith]] was sacked on 22 September 2024, with [[Neil Critchley]] replacing him as head coach a month later.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Club Statement: Steven Naismith – Hearts |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/club-statement-steven-naismith |access-date=2024-09-22 |website=www.heartsfc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Anderson |first=Barry |date=21 September 2024 |title=Hearts report and player ratings v St Mirren: Fans chant against Steven Naismith amid a critical situation |url=https://www.edinburghnews.scotsman.com/sport/football/hearts/hearts-report-and-player-ratings-v-st-mirren-fans-chant-against-steven-naismith-amid-a-critical-situation-4791710 |access-date=22 September 2024 |website=Edinburgh Evening News}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Neil Critchley named new Head Coach – Hearts |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/neil-critchley-named-new-head-coach |access-date=2024-10-15 |website=www.heartsfc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref>

After discussions with [[Brighton & Hove Albion F.C.|Brighton]] owner [[Tony Bloom]] throughout the [[2024–25 Scottish Premiership|2024–25 season]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=McLauchlin |first=Brian |date=2024-09-16 |title=Hearts & Brighton owner in talks over recruitment & possible investment |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c8j772z8medo |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=BBC Sport |language=en-GB}}</ref> on 20 November 2024 Hearts announced that they would become the first partner of Jamestown Analytics in Scotland, the same company used by Bloom's own Brighton in the [[Premier League]], [[Como 1907|Como]] in [[Serie A]] and [[Royale Union Saint-Gilloise]] in the [[Belgian Pro League]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Hearts partner with Jamestown Analytics |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/hearts-partner-with-jamestown-analytics |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=www.heartsfc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> The software was first used to appoint Critchley<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sked |first=Joel |date=2024-11-20 |title=Hearts confirm Jamestown Analytics partnership: Recruitment, analysis, Jones role |url=https://www.heartsstandard.co.uk/news/24737442.hearts-confirm-partnership-jamestown-analytics/ |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=Hearts Standard |language=en}}</ref> as head coach in October after Naismith had been sacked.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Club Statement: Steven Naismith – Hearts |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/club-statement-steven-naismith |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=www.heartsfc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-09-22 |title=Steven Naismith: Hearts sack head coach after eight successive defeats |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cdjeygg03meo |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=BBC Sport |language=en-GB}}</ref> Critchley was later sacked in April after failing to make the top six before the split.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McLauchlin |first=Brian |title=BBC Sport - How did Critchley's tenure unfold? |date=26 April 2025 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/articles/cly1pvv1dpdo}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Club Statement: Critchley & Garrity depart – Hearts |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/club-statement-critchley-garrity-depart-2 |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=www.heartsfc.co.uk |language=en}}</ref> On 25 June 2025, Hearts announced that [[Tony Bloom]] would officially join the Hearts board after completing a £10m investment, giving him a 29% stake in the club.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tony bloom investment complete |url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/tony-bloom-investment-complete}}</ref> Hearts began the [[2025–26 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2025–26 season]] with an unbeaten run under [[Derek McInnes]], including a 3–1 win over [[2024–25 Scottish Premiership]] winners [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Murray |first=Ewan |url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2025/oct/26/hearts-celtic-scottish-premiership-match-report |title=Hearts move eight points clear at top after Shankland spot-kick sees off Celtic |date=2025-10-26 |publisher=The Guardian }}</ref> The club remained at the top of the league for most of the 2025–26 campaign, but a 3–1 away defeat to Celtic on the final matchday saw them drop to second place.<ref>{{cite web |last=Binnie |first=Adam |url=https://www.skysports.com/football/news/11781/13544422/celtic-win-scottish-premiership-title-but-does-hearts-emergence-mean-the-scottish-football-landscape-has-changed-forever |title=Celtic win Scottish Premiership title but does Hearts' emergence mean the Scottish football landscape has changed forever? |publisher=Sky Sports |date=16 May 2026 }}</ref>

[[File:The Heart of Midlothian.JPG|thumb|220x220px|The ''[[Heart of Midlothian (Royal Mile)|Heart of Midlothian]]'' mosaic, on which the current club crest is based]]

The original Hearts [[football strip]] was all white shirts and trousers with maroon trimmings, and a heart sewn onto the chest.<ref name="historical kits"/> For one season they played in red, white and blue stripes.<ref name="historical kits"/> These were the colours of a club called St. Andrew, who had taken their name and colours from the [[University of St Andrews]], that Hearts had absorbed. Since then the predominant club colours have been maroon and white.<ref name="historical kits">{{cite web|url=http://www.historicalkits.co.uk/Scottish_Football_League/Heart_of_Midlothian/Heart_of_Midlothian.htm |title=Heart of Midlothian|publisher=Historical Football Kits |access-date=13 August 2011}}</ref> The strip typically has a maroon top and a white collar,<ref name="historical kits"/> although the strip was predominantly white in the 2010–11 season.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://sport.scotsman.com/sport/Revealed-Hearts39--radical-new.6426773.jp|title=Revealed: Hearts' radical new strip|work=[[Edinburgh Evening News]]|publisher=Johnston Press|date=19 July 2010|access-date=13 August 2011}}</ref> The club's [[2024-25 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2024-25]] home shirt was all-maroon.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.heartsfc.co.uk/blogs/news/24-25-home-kit-revealed |title=24/25 HOME KIT REVEALED |publisher=Heart of Midlothian F.C. |date=31 May 2024 |access-date=13 August 2024}}</ref> The shorts are normally white, although maroon shorts and socks are sometimes worn.<ref name="historical kits"/>

The badge is a heart, based on the ''[[Heart of Midlothian (Royal Mile)|Heart of Midlothian]]'' mosaic on the [[Royal Mile]]. There is a tradition to spit on the mosaic when passing, harking back to the days when the city jail stood there.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.timberbush-tours.co.uk/news-offers/the-story-of-scotlands-famous-heart/|title=Timberbush Tours - The Story of Scotland's Famous Heart|website=Timberbush-tours.co.uk|access-date=27 July 2018}}</ref>

For the [[2014–15 Heart of Midlothian F.C. season|2014–15]] season the club chose to commemorate 100 years since [[McCrae's Battalion]] with not only a commemorative strip, of maroon shirt, white shorts and black socks, but with a commemorative badge as well. The club chose to have no sponsor on the home top as a mark of respect to those who had joined the regiment.
